Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Layla was 18 when her younger brother, Sami, suddenly became critically ill, and the experience shattered the ordinary rhythm of her family’s life. One evening he had been laughing at the kitchen table, and by the next day he was in a hospital bed with monitors beeping around him, his small body seeming overwhelmed by the seriousness of what was happening. Layla remembered the hard, fluorescent light of the pediatric ward, the smell of antiseptic, and her mother’s face changing each time a doctor walked in. She stayed close to Sami, watching every movement, but she also felt acutely aware of how little she could do. When he became more frightened, she felt herself freeze, as if she were supposed to somehow make it stop and could not. In the months that followed, she came to see that moment as the point where something in her changed. Even after Sami recovered enough to come home, she could not return to feeling that the world was predictable.

By the time she began working in a warehouse, Layla was still carrying the strain of those months. The job was physically demanding and fast-paced, with shelves stacked high and carts rattling across the concrete floor, and she found herself on edge whenever a sudden sound cut through the hum of the building. A cart slamming into a metal frame, a sharp alarm, or the brief, startled cry of another worker could send a jolt through her body so quickly that her chest tightened and her hands went cold. She was embarrassed by how intense these reactions felt, especially because other people barely seemed to notice the same noises. At work she tried to push through, but she often caught herself losing her place in a task because her attention slipped away; one moment she would be checking labels, and the next she would realize she had stared at the same box for several seconds without taking in what she was seeing. The warehouse required constant focus, and she feared being seen as careless or not strong enough for the job, even though she was trying hard.

What frightened Layla most was how easily her mind went back to the hospital whenever something in the present resembled that time. If she saw a child with an IV pole in a waiting room, or heard someone mention a “scan” or “results,” a wave of fear would hit her before she could think. She would feel it physically first: her stomach dropping, her heart pounding, and a prickling tension moving through her arms and shoulders. She described those moments as if her body remembered before her mind caught up. Her emotions also rose quickly and intensely; she could feel fear, horror, and a sharp rush of guilt, sometimes all at once, particularly when she thought about how helpless Sami had looked and how distressed her mother had been. She had come to believe that she should have protected them somehow, that a better sister would have been calmer, stronger, or more useful. Instead, she remembered standing in the hospital corridor with her hands clenched, unable to do anything except watch. That memory still came with a heavy sense that she had failed at the very moment her family needed her most.

Over time, Layla’s view of herself became harsher. She often told herself that she was weak because she had been so shaken by an experience that others in her family seemed to talk about more matter-of-factly. She knew, rationally, that Sami had survived and was doing better now, yet emotionally she remained convinced that bad things could still happen without warning and that she would be unable to stop them. That sense of helplessness had become part of how she interpreted ordinary life: if a text message from her mother came in after a delay, or if someone looked worried, she immediately imagined the worst. She found herself scanning for signs that something was wrong, even when nothing obvious was happening, and she hated how quickly her body seemed to react before she could settle herself.

At home, the family had mostly returned to normal routines, but Layla had not fully returned with them. She still lived with the memory of the hospital as though it were close by, and she often kept her feelings to herself because she did not want to burden her parents with more worry. Her relationship had become one of the few places where she felt somewhat understood, although even there she struggled to explain why certain reminders could leave her shaken for hours. She finally sought help after a series of difficult shifts at the warehouse, when her concentration slips and physical startle reactions began to feel harder to hide. She was tired of feeling as though her own body were always braced for another emergency. What she wanted most was to stop feeling so easily overwhelmed by reminders of Sami’s illness, and what she feared most was that she would always believe she was weak and powerless whenever life suddenly turned frightening again.
